Learning Objectives
Review the epidemiology, etiology, and risk factors for osteoporotic fractures.
Review the appropriate workup for a patient with an osteoporotic fracture.
Determine the appropriate definitive treatment for a patient with an osteoporotic fracture.
Identify the risks and limitations of surgical management of osteoporotic fractures.
Discuss alternatives and adjuncts to the surgical treatment of patients with poor bone quality.
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Fractures of osteoporotic bone present unique challenges regarding perioperative medical
optimization, treatment principles, surgical fixation options, weight-bearing restrictions,

Epidemiology
More than 200 million people worldwide are affected by osteoporosis. Approximately 43
million people in the United States make up the current geriatric (>65 years) population, and
this number is expected to double to 83.7 million by 2050.
Approximately 9 million osteoporotic fractures occur each year, and this number expected to
double by 2040. Ninety percent of these osteoporotic fractures result from a low-energy fall
from a standing height.1 These fractures are associated with a high rate of morbidity and
mortality. In addition, the overall cost of management of these injuries is approximately $18
billion globally per year.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
With osteoporosis, a negative balance occurs between bone formation and bone resorption.
This leads to overall decreased bone density with the deterioration of the microarchitecture of
cortical and cancellous bone, which becomes considerably porous and thin.

Osteology
Cancellous bone is affected more than cortical bone, explaining the reason most
osteoporotic fractures occur in the metaphyseal region of bone that is mostly cancellous
bone. Therefore, the bone has decreased strength and has fewer and thinner bony
trabeculae. Because of this phenomenon, attaining good purchase via standard fixation
hardware and techniques is more difficult. A reduction in cortical thickness of 1 mm
leads to a 50% reduction in the holding power of a screw.1
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
90% of fractures result from a low-energy mechanism of injury, most commonly a fall from a
standing height or less.2

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Examples of common mechanisms of injury include a fall onto outstretched hand (distal
radius), a fall onto the hip (hip fracture, pelvic fracture), or a fall onto the buttock
(vertebral compression fracture, pelvic fracture). Vertebral compression fractures are the
most common type of osteoporotic fracture diagnosed, followed by hip fractures and
distal radius fractures (Figure 1). However, not all osteoporotic fractures result from a
low-energy mechanism of injury. Elderly patients can still sustain fractures from higher
energy trauma (ie, motor vehicle collisions, fall from a height, pedestrian struck) but with
the confounding factor of associated osteoporotic bone. The current financial burden of
geriatric trauma in the overall trauma population in the United States is 30%, and that
number will continue to increase.3

Risk Factors
Risk profiling of this elderly population requires accounting for energy mechanism of injury,
patient age, patient physiologic status, injury profile, history of fragility fracture, and
comorbidity status.
Certain lifestyles, medications, and medical comorbidities increased the risk for
osteopenia/osteoporosis.

Risk Factors
Prior fragility fracture is the strongest predictor of a future low-energy fracture.
Specifically, patients diagnosed with a vertebral compression fracture are five times
more likely to sustain a second vertebral compression fracture or hip fracture.4
A thorough patient history must be obtained to identify patients at higher risk. These risk
factors include a history of fracture in a first degree relative, certain genetic conditions,
female sex, advanced age, Caucasian race, cigarette smoking, low body mass index, low
calcium and/or vitamin D intake, excessive alcohol intake, sedentary lifestyle, recurrent
falls, estrogen deficiency, hypogonadism, cancer, hypovitaminosis D,
hyperparathyroidism, hyperthyroidism, malabsorption, liver disease, chronic renal
failure, chronic steroid use, anticonvulsants, antiretrovirals, selective serotonin reuptake
inhibitors, certain diuretics, among other factors.5
Associated Injuries
Many patients who suffer a fragility fracture have associated medical comorbidities that
increase the risks associated with anesthesia and undergoing a surgical procedure.
A thorough physical examination from head to toe is indicated because all bones in the body
are affected by osteoporosis and, therefore, a simple fall that results in a fracture in one area

of the body may commonly cause an associated fragility fracture elsewhere in the body that
may not be readily apparent to the patient or the examining physician.

Associated Injuries
Elderly osteoporotic patients have a decreased ability to physiologically respond to these
types of injuries and a lower functional reserve to compensate if an injury occurs.
Commonly, comorbidities in this patient population include cardiac disease, renal
disease, pulmonary disease, malnutrition, and dementia. In addition, many older adults
are being treated with anticoagulant agents for various conditions. This, in combination
with an increased risk for falls, may lead to an increased risk for head trauma and
intracranial bleeding, which must be diagnosed and considered.
Injury Classification
A fragility fracture is defined as a fracture sustained during a fall from a standing height or less
(ie, low-energy mechanism of injury)
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History/Physical Examination
A thorough patient history and physical examination is important to diagnose the presenting
injury and to determine associated comorbidities that often determine the patient survival and
ultimate level of functional recovery from the injury.
The practitioner must identify and manage correctable causes of poor bone quality; otherwise,
these patients may have impaired recovery from the presenting injury and an increased risk
for future fragility fractures.
A detailed patient history also may identify an underlying malignancy, which must always be
included in the differential diagnosis for patients presenting with an atraumatic or low-energy
fracture.


Patient History/Physical Examination
In this patient population, the prevalence of dementia to varying degrees is increased,
and a thorough patient history may not be able to be elucidated from patients
themselves. In such a case, caregivers, loved ones, and previous medical records may be
invaluable in obtaining an appropriate background on a patient.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
The initial survey of a suspected fracture is almost always via plain radiographs. Orthogonal
views of the involved bone must be obtained.
Radiographs of the joint above and below the level of injury must be obtained to ensure no
associated fractures or dislocations are present.

Radiography
Common findings of advanced osteoporosis include thin cortices and a loss of
trabeculae (Figure 2). Approximately 30% to 50% bone loss is required to appreciate
decreased bone mass on plain radiographs. A common osteoporotic fracture is a
vertebral compression fracture, which may present as loss of height or kyphosis of the
spine because of a wedging effect; however, two-thirds of vertebral compression
fractures are asymptomatic or minimally symptomatic and may be found incidentally on
routine imaging studies for other pathology.

Computed Tomography
CT may be especially useful in patients with periarticular injuries to identify intra-
articular fracture lines and comminution and to further delineate the fracture pattern for
surgical planning. This may aid in the decision-making process with regard to whether
fixation can be achieved or if joint replacement is necessary.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI may be helpful in the diagnosis of nondisplaced or minimally displaced low-energy
fractures that are not apparent on plain radiographs or CT scans (Figure 4).

Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI usually will reveal bony edema (increased signal on T2-weighted images) within the
bone in question if the fracture is acute. MRI is especially useful in the diagnosis of a
nondisplaced hip fracture or to assess for propagation of an isolated greater trochanter

fracture, of which 90% will show extension into the intertrochanteric region. MRI may
help the treating physician determine the acuity of vertebral compression fractures. It
also may be especially valuable in the diagnosis of pelvic and sacral insufficiency
fractures.
Bone Scintigraphy
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry is the preferred method for measuring bone mineral
density.

Bone Scintigraphy
The World Health Organization reports and defines bone mineral density measurements
in relation to the T-score, which is relative to normal, young matched controls.
Osteopenia is defined as a T-score of -1 to -2.5 standard deviations and osteoporosis is
defined as a T-score of <-2.5 standard deviations.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Fracture Stabilization
If indicated, nonsurgical fracture management is similar to that for non-osteoporotic fractures.

Fracture Stabilization
Well-padded splints in the acute period can be transitioned to a well-molded cast as
swelling allows. Because of poor bone quality and commonly substantial comminution at
fracture ends, these patients must be followed closely to ensure maintenance of
reduction and alignment.

12/30

Outcomes
Certain fracture types, namely distal radius fractures, can be allowed to unite with a
considerable amount of displacement with little functional deficit.6
Isolated displaced fractures of the olecranon in low-demand elderly patients, which in a
younger patient population would be indicated for surgical management, are associated with
satisfactory short- and long-term outcomes with nonsurgical management.7
Surgical Management
The success of surgical management depends on multiple factors, some of which are within a
surgeon’s control.
The treating surgeon also should have a thorough understanding of the biomechanics of
osteoporotic fracture fixation principles, which are complicated by various factors.

Surgical Management
These factors include whether the fracture is articular, metaphyseal, or diaphyseal and
whether or a simple fracture line or considerable comminution is present. The soft-
tissue envelope is important to consider in determining surgical fixation strategies
because elderly patients often have decreased muscle mass and frail skin. Associated
fractures and injuries may influence the surgical plan and timing. The patient’s overall
physiologic status must be considered. Associated comorbidities must be identified and
weighed during the planning process. Current medication lists should be sought because
many medications may influence fracture and wound healing.
These factors include the presence of comminuted metaphyseal patterns; short articular
segments, commonly with intra-articular comminution; the decreased holding power of
screws in osteoporotic bone; and the material properties of various implant options with
regard to stability and flexibility (Resource 2).
Indications
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:37 PM
AAOS | Management of Osteoporotic Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6002025
13/30

Surgical indications for many fractures in elderly patients are similar to those in patients with a
non-osteoporotic fracture.
Depending on the type of fracture, early surgical treatment of elderly patients with an
osteoporotic fragility fracture is important if the patient is medically optimized by a
hospitalist/geriatrician.

Indications
For example, hip fracture fixation within 24 to 48 hours is associated with decreased
major and minor complications.8 Early surgical management reduces immobilization and
deconditioning in this already vulnerable patient population. Most pelvic ring/sacral
fractures in patients with osteoporosis result from low-energy trauma and typically are
stable, allowing them to be managed nonsurgically; however, the clinical course of these
fractures may be variable, with a considerable portion of patients having sustained pain,
which limits activity and mobilization. In these patients, a minimally invasive procedure,
such as the placement of a trans-sacral screw or other surgical fixation option, should be
considered to impart stability to the pelvis and allow for mobilization and earlier
resolution of pain.9-11
Contraindications
A surgical procedure to fix an otherwise surgical fracture pattern may be contraindicated in
patients who are in the final stages of life, in whom palliative care is better indicated. This
decision must be determined via a multidisciplinary approach.
Surgical treatment may be contraindicated in patients who cannot tolerate surgical treatment
or anesthesia because of medical comorbidities.
Surgical management may be contraindicated for certain fracture types that result in
acceptable outcomes if managed nonsurgically in the elderly population that may, in younger
counterparts, be indicated for surgical management; examples include certain distal radius
and proximal humerus fractures.12,13
Techniques/Procedures

14/30

Preoperative Planning
Preoperative identification and optimization of comorbidities should be managed via an
interdisciplinary fashion following best-practice guidelines to optimize efficiency and value-
based care.
Preoperative physical status assessment is a key component of the preoperative risk
assessment for geriatric patients with a fracture.
The role of interdisciplinary care for geriatric trauma patients has been adopted by the
American College of Surgeons.

Preoperative Planning
A widely used and accepted physical status classification system is the American Society
of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Classification System (Resource 3). American Society
of Anesthesiologists class alone has been shown to correlate with risk of complications,
readmission, and inpatient mortality.14 A preoperative functional status assessment is
helpful in determining perioperative cardiac risk. Functional status is a measure of a
patient’s ability to perform routine physical activity without decompensating.
Preoperative optimization of geriatric trauma patients with considerable medical
comorbidities should be performed in conjunction with a medical specialist or a
geriatrician. Co-management of geriatric trauma patients by an orthopaedic surgeon and
a geriatrician is associated with decreased hospital length of stay, decreased
readmission rates, decreased time to surgical management, decreased complication
rates, and decreased inpatient mortality rates.15,16 Implementation of fracture liaison
service also has been shown to decrease the mortality rate by 35% and decrease the risk
for subsequent nonvertebral fracture by 56% over a 2-year period.17
Patient Positioning
Positioning of a patient for surgical treatment depends on the type of fracture, surgical
approach to be used, type of imaging to be used, the patient’s physiologic status (anesthesia
requirements), associated injuries, and surgeon preference.

Complications associated with improper patient positioning include skin irritation and
pressure ulcers, nerve injury/palsy, compartment syndrome, hypothermia, stroke, and
blindness.18,19

Patient Positioning
Regardless of the position used, all bony prominences must be well padded to prevent
skin irritation. A radiolucent table should be used to facilitate intraoperative imaging for
assessment of fracture reduction and stabilization. Unless contraindicated, sequential
compression devices should be applied to the lower extremities (unless the limb is
undergoing surgical management), and a forced-air warming device should be used to
prevent perioperative hypothermia. If the surgical procedure is expected to be of long
duration, the placement of a Foley catheter should be considered before starting the
procedure.
Surgical Approaches
The surgical approach depends on the location of the fracture, the fracture pattern, and the
planned fixation option (ie, internal fixation versus replacement). The approach can be a
formal open incision, a minimally invasive incision, a percutaneous option, and or a combined
approach.
Surgical fracture fixation strategy—A key tenet of osteoporotic fracture fixation is one-shot
surgery to avoid revision surgery

Surgical Approaches
Regardless of the surgical approach used, the goal is to attain the appropriate access
necessary to fully assess and understand the fracture pattern and perform definitive
fixation while limiting the surgical insult, being as tissue-friendly as possible.
The maintenance of stability of osteoporotic fractures occurs via impaction at the
fracture site, functional fracture reduction, splinting of the fracture over a long area, and

16/30

the use of materials to augment the strength of the bone if necessary.20 Fixed-angle
devices can help create stability for the fracture because of their mechanical
properties.21 Arthroplasty may be an alternative in select situations.22
The treating surgeon should plan ahead and anticipate complications associated with
internal fixation, especially involving osteoporotic bone. Because of the difficulty and
complications associated with fixation in these fracture types, the surgeon should have a
backup plan in the event that the first surgical fixation option does not work as planned.
This may involve conversion to an arthroplasty option midway through the procedure;
therefore, the appropriate implants and instruments must be readily available.
Plate Fixation
Poor bone quality results in poor bone purchase with the use of standard fixation hardware;
the use of larger diameter screws with greater surface contact area; screws that allow for
bicortical purchase; angular stable constructs, such as blade plates; locking technology; and
hardware that is designed to provide more load-bearing rather than load-sharing is
recommended23,24 (Resource 4).
Locking plates allow for the threads of the screw head to lock into accepting threads in the
plate to create a fixed-angle construct, obviating the need for a friction fit between the plate
and bone. The load is transferred through the screws and the interface between the screw and
the plate. Individual screws are theoretically prevented from toggling and cutting through the
bone.

Plate Fixation
Traditional nonlocking plates rely on friction of the plate on the bone by compressing
screws, which induces a large amount of preload on the bone immediately around the
screw, increasing the risk for pullout. The load is then transferred from the bone to the
plate across the fracture site and back to the bone again (load-bearing construct). The
smooth undersurface of the screw heads in the plate also are able to toggle with

micromotion of the segment. Locking plate technology provides improved performance
in osteoporotic bone compared with traditional nonlocking plates21 (Resource 5).
Intramedullary Nails
Newer generations of intramedullary nails have expanded indications beyond diaphyseal
fractures, allowing for fixation in metaphyseal region and certain periarticular fractures. Nails
are ideal for many osteoporotic fractures for many reasons.
Newer-generation nails also have improved and expanded interlocking designs to allow for
improved fixation and stability.
Although intramedullary nails provide certain biologic and biomechanical advantages, fracture
reduction and fixation may be technically demanding. Clinically, the outcomes with nails for
many fractures are not superior compared with those of plate fixation.

Intramedullary Nails
Intramedullary nails often can be placed percutaneously without the need for a formal,
large open incision, protecting the soft tissues and blood supply around the fracture site.
Intramedullary nails are implanted closer to the mechanical axis of the bone and,
therefore, have a higher resistance to bending forces. Nails are load-sharing devices that
allow the forces to be more equally distributed between the implant and native bone
over a longer segment, acting as an internal splint to allow for secondary bone healing.25
Large-diameter interlocking screws and helical blades are available. Certain screws can
lock into the nail. Many nail designs have an increased number of interlocking screw
options in each segment of bone to maximize the purchase in short-segment fractures.
They also are configured in multiple planes to allow for improved stability to varying
stresses. End caps of certain manufacturers can turn the most distal/proximal screw into
a locked screw within the nail, reducing screw toggle. Blocking and/or cortical-replacing
screws can be used to manage malalignment and increase the stability of the
construct.26

Augmentation
Bone cement (polymethyl methacrylate or calcium phosphate), which was originally used in
the ophthalmologic and dental fields, has an expanded role in orthopaedics. Bone cement can
be injected into screw holes or the canal of long bones to improve screw purchase and
strength at the bone-implant interface.
Adverse effects and complications of bone cement use in fracture fixation include extrusion of
cement into adjacent tissues or joints, thermal necrosis, hypotension, infection, complicated
future surgical procedure, and extrusion into the fracture site that hinders fracture healing.36-
38
Allograft cortical struts may be used to provide additional structural cortex to hold screws or
stabilize cerclage wires/cables.
The use of allograft bone is not without risks. Adverse effects and complications associated
with the use of cadaver bone include infection risk, cost, limited availability, and unpredictable
incorporation that may complicate future revision procedures.41

Augmentation
Cement has poor bone adhesion properties, but it intrudes into the cancellous structure
of bone (similar to grout) and results in much stronger composite after polymerization.27
Some orthopaedic fields that commonly use cement augmentation include arthroplasty
to stabilize components within the bone, spine surgery to improve pedicle screw
pullout28,29 and to manage vertebral fractures via kyphoplasty,30 and trauma surgery.31
Specific fractures include hip fractures. A biomechanical study on proximal femur
cadaver model fixation via traditional systems augmented with polymethyl methacrylate
reported a 50% lower failure rate compared with nonaugmented femusr.32 Use of
cement in the management of tibial plateau fractures has been well documented to fill
bone voids33,34 and has shown promise in enhancing implant/screw anchorage into the
humeral head of proximal humerus fractures.35
Allograft cortical struts were classically used for the management of periprosthetic
femur fractures39 with poor bone stock. This method has fallen out of favor with the
advent of locking plates but is an option. Allograft struts also can be used to augment

Arthroplasty
Acute arthroplasty has been mainly used to manage intra-articular fractures because of poor
subchondral bone quality, impaction, substantial comminution, and inability to maintain
reduction. It also can be used to manage fractures with an elevated risk for osteonecrosis,
such as femoral neck and proximal humerus fractures.
Primary arthroplasty allows for immediate–weight bearing and early mobilization in most
patients, which is of paramount importance in the geriatric patient population as previously
discussed.
An instructional course lecture by Schmidt et al22 reviews the role of immediate arthroplasty in
geriatric trauma (Resource 6).

Arthroplasty

Delayed arthroplasty for certain fracture types in trauma patients is associated with
poorer outcomes than arthroplasty for the management of primary osteoarthritis,42,43
likely because of delayed mobilization leading to deconditioning, joint stiffness, various
medical complications, and an altered surgical field at time of definitive surgical fixation.
A steep learning curve may be associated with these complex periarticular injuries;
examples include acetabular fractures managed via total hip arthroplasty alone or in
combination with open reduction and internal fixation;44 distal humerus fractures
managed via total elbow arthroplasty;45 distal femur fractures managed via total knee
arthroplasty or distal femur replacement;46 and proximal humerus fractures managed
via hemiarthroplasty, total shoulder arthroplasty, or reverse total shoulder
arthroplasty.47
Postoperative Management
A primary goal of surgical fixation of lower extremity fractures in elderly patients with
osteoporosis is early mobilization with weight bearing. Therefore, ideal fixation involves the
use of a construct that will allow the patient to fully bear weight on the surgical side.
Priority also should be given to the prevention of future falls.
After a hip fracture, a patient has a 10% to 14% risk for another fracture each year.49
Supplementation with calcium and vitamin D is an effective method of preventing fractures,
and possibly falls, regardless of bone mineral density or fracture history.50 All patients with a
fragility fracture should receive supplementation based on their serum levels as proposed by
Bukata et al.23
Postoperatively, the goal should be discharge from the hospital to a safe environment decided
on by a multidisciplinary team consisting of the patient, the patient’s family, a social worker,
the orthopaedist, a physical therapist, and the geriatrician/hospitalist to decrease overall
morbidity and mortality, increase functional status, decrease pain, and prevent future
readmission.

Postoperative Management

Prolonged periods of reduced weight bearing and immobilization are associated with
high morbidity. In addition, most elderly patients will not be able to fully comply with
weight-bearing restrictions because of physical or cognitive reasons; this must be
considered in surgical planning and in selecting fixation options.48
Discharge location may range from the home with minimal assistance to an acute care
facility. The Score for Trauma Triage in the Geriatric and Middle-Aged is a validated
mortality risk index for middle-aged and geriatric trauma patients that is used to predict
discharge location in a cohort of elderly patients with a low-energy hip fracture, with
successful discharge planning measured by readmission rates.51
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Complications
Nonunion
In older adults, the rate of nonunion and implant failure is higher than in the younger
population, with a reported rate of 2% to 10% with certain fractures.52,53
Malunion
Malunion varies depending on fracture location and treatment option but has been reported
to occur in 4% to 40% of patients, depending on anatomic location.52,53
Hardware Failure
Internal fixation failure in osteoporotic bone typically results from bone failure rather than
implant breakage (as in patients with good bone quality), which results in cutout, fracture
subsidence, or plate pull-off.

Hardware Failure

Failed fixation occurs in 2% to 10% of certain osteoporotic fractures.52,53 With
osteoporotic femoral neck fractures managed via internal fixation, failure may occur in
as many as 30% to 40% of patients (Resource 7).
Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
The rate of deep vein thrombosis after hip fracture is as high as 40% without prophylaxis,49
and older age is an independent risk factor for deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism
after injury.54 Various medical societies have published deep vein thrombosis prophylaxis
guidelines including the American College of Chest Physicians55 and the Eastern Association
for the Surgery of Trauma.56

Deep Vein Thrombosis/Venous Thromboembolism
Communication with a geriatrician/medical team is essential to create a safe
postoperative/postinjury anticoagulation regimen in this vulnerable patient population
at high risk for deep vein thrombosis/pulmonary embolism and also at risk for falls and
subsequent trauma/bleeding. Patient comorbidities, history of anticoagulation, and
current medications must be considered.
Other Complications
Revision surgery rates in elderly patients with a minimally displaced femoral neck fracture are
associated with a relative risk reduction of 70% if managed via hemiarthroplasty compared to
internal fixation.57
The 1-month perioperative mortality associated with a hip fracture has been demonstrated to
be 10%. In female patients, mortality rates at 1 year are 25%, and 1-year mortality rates in men
may be as high as 30%.58
Perioperative mortality in elderly patients with a distal femur fracture is similar to that of hip
fractures.

Other Complications
Mortality at 1 year is 13.4%; if surgical management occurs more than 2 days postinjury,
the mortality rate is substantially increased at 30 days, 6 months, and 1-year time points
compared with surgical management performed less than 2 days postinjury.59 In a
review of 92 consecutive patients older than 60 years with a low-energy supracondylar
distal femur fracture, Streubel et al60 reported that these fractures were associated with
a mortality rate similar to hip fractures in elderly patients. The authors also reported that
a surgical delay of more than 4 days further increased the 6-month and 1-year mortality
rates. Rozental et al61 reported that, 7 years after an elderly patient sustained a distal
radius fracture, the cumulative estimated survival was 57% compared with an expected
value of 71% for the U.S. population.
